content: Nasal Polyp Diagnosis History and Symptoms Nasal polyps are often asymptomatic, particularly when they are small, and may be discovered incidentally during an examination. However, larger polyps or clusters can lead to significant symptoms, including nasal obstruction, loss of smell (anosmia) or taste, nasal congestion, facial pain or headaches, sneezing, rhinorrhea (runny nose), postnasal drip, itching around the eyes, and snoring. Pathophysiology Although nasal polyps are considered idiopathic, frequent infections and chronic inflammation are thought to contribute to their development. These polyps typically originate from the mucosal lining of the ethmoidal or maxillary sinuses. Histopathological analysis reveals epithelial damage, edema, fibrosis, hyperplastic or metaplastic epithelial changes, and thickening of the basement membrane. Nasal polyps are rich in inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, mast cells, and T lymphocytes, as well as cytokines, chemokines, interleukins, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and adhesion molecules. Genetic predispositions have also been implicated, with studies identifying specific genes and single nucleotide polymorphisms (e.g., RYD5) associated with the condition. Individuals expressing the HLA-DQA10201-DQB10201 haplotype have a 5.53-fold increased risk of developing nasal polyps. Impaired mucosal innate immunity and weakened immune responses further contribute to the pathogenesis. Carbonic anhydrase (CA), a zinc metalloenzyme responsible for water and electrolyte transport across the epithelium, is downregulated in nasal polyps, contributing to edema. Genetic studies on CA expression may aid in diagnosis and management. Fungal particles, which are typically harmless in healthy individuals, can act as antigens in immunocompromised patients, triggering eosinophilic inflammation. Superinfections may arise from germinating fungal spores, while fungal irritants (e.g., Aspergillus and Alternaria species) can exacerbate nasal polyposis. Etiology The exact cause of nasal polyps remains unclear, but they are a common condition affecting approximately 4% of the population. Nasal polyps are frequently associated with other conditions, including aspirin sensitivity (36%), asthma (7%), cystic fibrosis (20%), and chronic rhinosinusitis. Other related conditions include Churg-Strauss syndrome (eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis), allergic fungal sinusitis, ciliary dyskinesia syndromes (e.g., Kartagener's syndrome), Young syndrome, and nasal mastocytosis. Nasal polyps are more prevalent in non-allergic asthma compared to allergic asthma. In children, cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of nasal polyps. Any child aged 12–20 years presenting with nasal polyps should be evaluated for cystic fibrosis, as approximately 50% of individuals with cystic fibrosis develop extensive polyps that may require aggressive management. Differential Diagnosis Nasal polyps can resemble other nasal masses, necessitating careful differentiation. Benign masses include encephalocele, glioma, antrochoanal polyp, angiofibroma, and inverted papilloma. Malignant masses include squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), esthesioneuroblastoma, nasal lymphoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma. Epidemiology Nasal polyposis is a common condition, affecting 1–4% of the population. It is more prevalent in men than women and is most commonly diagnosed between the ages of 40 and 60. While the exact etiology is unknown, genetic predispositions and associations with asthma and chronic rhinosinusitis have been identified. Patients with chronic rhinosinusitis, particularly allergic fungal rhinosinusitis, have a 10–54% prevalence of nasal polyps. Aspirin sensitivity is associated with nasal polyps in 40–80% of cases, and cystic fibrosis in 36%. Children with nasal polyps should undergo mandatory cystic fibrosis screening. Classification 1. Primary Classification Ethmoidal Polyps: Common in adults, these small, grape-like masses originate from the ethmoidal sinuses and extend into the middle meatus. Antrochoanal Polyps: More common in children, these large, solitary polyps originate from the maxillary sinus and extend posteriorly into the choana, sometimes hanging behind the soft palate. 2. Histopathological Classification Eosinophilic Edematous (Allergic): The most common type, characterized by epithelial edema, goblet cell hyperplasia, basement membrane thickening, and an abundance of eosinophils and leukocytes. Fibroinflammatory: Resulting from chronic inflammation and epithelial metaplasia. Polyp with Hyperplasia of Seromucinous Glands: Rare. Polyp with Atypical Stroma: Rare. 3. Phenotypical Classification of Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps Eosinophilic Neutrophilic Non-Eosinophilic, Non-Neutrophilic Otosclerosis Overview Otosclerosis, derived from the Greek word sklērós (hardening) and oto (ear), is a condition characterized by abnormal bone remodeling in the otic capsule. The dense endochondral bone of the labyrinth is replaced by irregularly laid spongy bone, leading to stapes fixation and impaired sound transmission at the oval window. While most cases involve the oval window, otosclerosis can also affect the round window, cochlear apex, internal auditory canal, cochlear aqueduct, semicircular canals, and stapes footplate. Advanced cases may extend into the bony labyrinth, causing mixed conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. Otosclerosis is more common in Caucasians and predominantly affects women. Hormonal fluctuations, such as those during pregnancy or menopause, may exacerbate the condition. Genetic factors play a significant role, with autosomal dominant inheritance and incomplete penetrance. Measles infection and inflammatory cytokines have also been implicated. Treatment primarily involves stapes surgery, which has a high success rate (90–95% improvement within the first five years). Hearing aids and cochlear implants may also be used. Pathophysiology Otosclerosis results from increased bone remodeling, involving resorption followed by deposition of abnormal bone in the otic capsule. Lesions are most commonly found anterior to the oval window, calcifying the annular ligament or stapes footplate (80%). Other sites include the round window (30%), pericochlear region (21%), and anterior internal auditory canal (19%). Bone remodeling occurs in three phases, and the extent of remodeling correlates with audiological findings. Etiology The exact cause of otosclerosis remains unknown, but potential etiologies include genetic predisposition, trauma, major surgeries, and inflammatory mediators. Measles infection has also been implicated. Epidemiology Otosclerosis is an autosomal dominant condition with incomplete penetrance, with 60% of patients reporting a family history. It is more common in women (2:1 ratio) and typically begins in the second or third decade of life, with hearing loss manifesting in the fourth decade. The clinical prevalence is higher in Caucasians (0.04–1%), with histological incidence reaching 10%. In African and Asian populations, histological incidence is 1% and 5%, respectively. Diagnosis Physical Examination Tuning Fork Tests: Negative Rinne test (conductive hearing loss). Weber test lateralizes to the ear with more severe conductive loss. Audiometry and Tympanometry Carhart’s Notch: A characteristic dip in bone conduction thresholds at 2000 Hz, which resolves after stapedectomy. Tympanometry is normal in early disease but shows flattening and stiffening in advanced cases, indicating low compliance of the ossicular chain and tympanic membrane. CT Imaging High-resolution CT of the temporal bones is the imaging modality of choice, showing increased bony radiolucency in the otic capsule, thickened stapes, and widening of the oval window. The halo sign (demineralized area outlining the cochlea) is an early finding. Treatment Medical Management: Sodium fluoride (controversial) to slow disease progression. Bisphosphonates to induce osteoclastic apoptosis and reduce bone resorption. Surgical Management: Stapedotomy or stapedectomy with prosthesis placement is the gold standard, with a high success rate. Revision surgery may be necessary for prosthesis displacement, persistent vertigo, or facial nerve damage. Hearing Aids: Used alone or in combination with surgery. Prognosis Most patients experience significant hearing improvement after surgery. Rarely, hearing loss may worsen, or prosthesis displacement may occur, necessitating revision surgery.
